content: A pressure ulcer, also known as a bedsore or decubitus ulcer, is a localized injury to the skin and underlying tissue that occurs when prolonged pressure is applied to the skin, reducing blood flow to the area and causing tissue damage. Symptoms of a Pressure Ulcer: Initially, a pressure ulcer appears as reddened skin that does not blanch (turn white) when pressed. This is the earliest sign of tissue damage. Over time, the affected area may develop a blister, which can progress to an open sore and eventually form a deep crater. Pressure ulcers most commonly develop over bony prominences where the skin is close to the bone, such as the elbows, heels, hips, ankles, shoulders, back, and the back of the head. Pressure ulcers are classified into four stages based on severity: Stage I: Reddened skin that does not blanch when pressed, indicating the beginning of tissue damage. Stage II: The skin forms a blister or an open sore, and the surrounding area may appear red and irritated. Stage III: The ulcer deepens, resembling a crater, with damage extending to the tissue beneath the skin. Stage IV: The ulcer becomes so deep that it damages muscles, bones, tendons, and sometimes joints. Causes of Pressure Ulcers: Pressure ulcers develop when constant pressure on the skin reduces blood supply to the area, leading to tissue death. This can occur when an individual remains in one position for an extended period without shifting their weight. People who use wheelchairs or are confined to bed, even for short periods (e.g., after surgery or an injury), are at risk. Risk Factors: Being bedridden or using a wheelchair. Advanced age. Limited mobility due to conditions such as spinal cord or brain injuries, or diseases like multiple sclerosis. Chronic conditions like diabetes or vascular disease, which impair blood flow. Mental disabilities, such as those caused by Alzheimer’s disease. Fragile or thin skin. Urinary or bowel incontinence. Malnutrition or inadequate nourishment. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if a blister or open sore develops on the skin. Seek immediate medical care if there are signs of infection, as infections can spread to other parts of the body and cause severe complications. Signs of an infected ulcer include: A foul odor from the ulcer. Redness and tenderness around the ulcer. Warm, swollen skin near the ulcer. Fever, weakness, or confusion, which may indicate that the infection has spread to the bloodstream or other areas. Treatment Options: Relieve pressure on the affected area using pillows, special foam cushions, or sheepskin to reduce pressure. Treat the ulcer based on its stage. A healthcare provider will provide specific instructions for care. Avoid further injury or friction to the area. Lightly powder bed sheets to reduce friction, and use medical supplies designed for this purpose. Improve nutrition and address any underlying issues that may hinder the healing process. For Stage II or more severe ulcers, follow your healthcare provider’s instructions for cleaning and caring for open wounds to prevent infection. Keep the area clean and free of dead tissue. Pressure ulcers are typically rinsed with a saline solution to remove loose, dead tissue. The wound should be covered with specialized gauze dressings designed for pressure ulcers. New medications that promote skin healing may be prescribed by your doctor. What Not to Do: Do not massage the area of the ulcer, as this can cause further damage to the underlying tissue. Avoid using donut-shaped or ring-shaped cushions, as they can interfere with blood flow and lead to complications. Prevention of Pressure Ulcers: If you are bedridden or have limited mobility due to conditions like diabetes, circulation problems, incontinence, or mental disabilities, check your skin daily for signs of pressure ulcers. Pay close attention to areas where pressure ulcers commonly form. Look for reddened areas that do not blanch when pressed, as well as blisters, sores, or craters. Take the following steps to prevent pressure ulcers: Change your position at least every two hours to relieve pressure. Use items like pillows, sheepskin, foam padding, and powders from medical supply stores to reduce pressure. Eat a well-balanced diet with sufficient calories to maintain health. Stay hydrated by drinking 8 to 10 cups of water daily. Exercise daily, including range-of-motion exercises. Keep the skin clean and dry. After urination or bowel movements, clean the area thoroughly and dry it well. A doctor may recommend creams to protect the skin.
